terroir.climate: Hot, dry Mediterranean, the sunniest and one of the driest regions of Italy, with rain concentrated in winter and summers that run past 35 degrees. The saving graces are wind and water: breezes from the Adriatic on one side and the Ionian on the other cross the narrow Salento, and the Murge plateau's modest altitude cools the nights at Gioia del Colle and Castel del Monte. Drought is the hazard; irrigation is now allowed and used.
terroir.soils: Limestone underlies the whole region, and over it lies terra rossa, the iron rich red clay that colours the Salento and the Murge; sand along the Ionian coast at Manduria; calcareous tufo and thin stony soils on the Murge; deeper alluvial soils on the Tavoliere plain in the north.
terroir.topography: The flattest region in Italy: the Tavoliere plain of Foggia, the Gargano promontory, the long limestone plateau of the Murge running down the middle at 300 to 500 metres, the Valle d'Itria of trulli houses, and the Salento peninsula, almost at sea level between the Adriatic and the Ionian. Hardly a vineyard rises above 500 metres.
terroir.water: Two seas: the Adriatic on the east and the Ionian in the gulf of Taranto to the west, with the Salento a narrow bridge between them. The Ofanto in the north is the one river of size; the rest of the region drinks from aqueducts, and the vineyards rely on the sea breezes for cool.

traps: Primitivo di Manduria DOC is dry; the DOCG with the same name is Dolce Naturale, the sweet one. Say which you mean.
Negroamaro means black bitter, or black black by another reading; it is not Aglianico and not Nero d'Avola.
Nero di Troia is a Puglian grape most likely named for the town of Troia near Foggia; Homer's Troy is a legend, not a provenance.
Tribidrag is Primitivo under its oldest Croatian name, not its parent; the older course note was loose. The parent idea belongs to Plavac Mali, Tribidrag's child.
Castel del Monte Bombino Nero is a DOCG for rosato alone, the only one in Italy; do not file it with the reds.
Primitivo ripens first, which is what the name means; it is not a primitive or ancient vine in any special sense.
Salice Salentino is a village and a DOC in the Salento; Salento itself is the peninsula and an IGT.
Puglia makes mostly red and rosato; its white Locorotondo is a Verdeca wine, not a Fiano.

wines.note: Deep, ripe and warm, blackberry jam, dried fig, cocoa and sweet spice at fourteen per cent and more, with soft tannin and a plush finish; the Riserva takes two years. Lamb, grilled sausages, aubergine parmigiana, or the cheese course.
The DOCG: Primitivo from late picked or dried bunches fermented to a sweet, strong red of prune and chocolate, poured in a small glass with chocolate or aged cheese.
Primitivo from the Murge plateau at around 300 to 500 metres: fresher, less jammy and more savoury than Manduria, with sour cherry and firmer acidity from the cool nights on limestone.
Negroamaro led with Malvasia Nera: dark plum, dried herbs, a bitter chocolate edge and soft grip, the Riserva after two years. Orecchiette with turnip tops and sausage, lamb and roasted peppers.

Negroamaro bled off its skins after a night's contact, deep coral and dry with cherry and bitter orange; Italy's oldest bottled rosato tradition, from 1943, and the region's best match for its fish and vegetable table.
A DOCG of structured, violet scented red from the Murge around the Swabian castle, firmer and longer lived than the Salento reds, with two years of ageing.
wines.style: Castel del Monte Nero di Troia Riserva

wines.note: A pale, dry rosato DOCG from the Bombino Nero grape, the only DOCG in Italy given to a rosato alone; light cherry and citrus, for the aperitivo and the antipasti.
A light, dry white of Verdeca and Bianco d'Alessano from the Valle d'Itria, neutral and crisp, the trulli country's wine with fresh burrata and raw seafood.

exam: Cannonau is Grenache (Garnacha); Cannonau di Sardegna DOC asks 85 per cent, Riserva two years, with Classico, Jerzu, Oliena and Capo Ferrato as sub-zones.
Vermentino di Gallura is the island's only DOCG (1996), 95 per cent Vermentino on granite in the north east; Vermentino di Sardegna is the DOC everywhere else.
Carignano del Sulcis: Carignan on ungrafted bush vines in the sand of the south west, DOC 1977; Terre Brune as the benchmark.
Vernaccia di Oristano: the island's first DOC (1971), a flor aged, sherry like dry white of 15 per cent, nothing to do with Vernaccia di San Gimignano.
Spanish rule from the fourteenth to the eighteenth century explains the grapes: Cannonau, Carignano, Monica, Bovale, Torbato.
Turriga as the famous IGT blend; Isola dei Nuraghi as the IGT name; Sella & Mosca and Argiolas as the two houses that modernised the island.
The geography: granite in the Gallura, sand in the Sulcis, the Gennargentu mountains, the Campidano plain, the maestrale wind, Corsica across the strait.

grapes.name: Grenache / Garnacha
grapes.styles: Cannonau on this island: the signature red, warm, herbal and high in alcohol with red fruit and soft tannin, from the mountains of Nuoro and Ogliastra at its best; Cannonau di Sardegna DOC covers the whole island.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: The white of the island, saline and citrus scented with a bitter almond finish; Vermentino di Gallura on granite is the DOCG and the fullest, Vermentino di Sardegna the lighter DOC everywhere else.

grapes.name: Carignan
grapes.styles: Carignano in the Sulcis of the south west, grown as old ungrafted bush vines on coastal sand: dark, savoury, plum and dried herb with soft tannin, and far finer than the grape's reputation in France.

grapes.name: Monica
grapes.styles: A soft, light, everyday red said to be Spanish in origin, Monica di Sardegna DOC, drunk young and often blended.

grapes.name: Bovale
grapes.styles: Two grapes under one name, Bovale Sardo and Bovale Grande, thought to have come from Spain, that give colour and tannin to blends such as Turriga and Mandrolisai.

grapes.name: Vernaccia di Oristano
grapes.styles: A white of the Tirso plain unrelated to Tuscany's Vernaccia, aged for years under flor in old chestnut and oak casks into a dry, nutty, sherry like wine of at least fifteen per cent.

grapes.name: Nuragus
grapes.styles: An ancient white of the Cagliari plain, perhaps Phoenician, neutral and crisp; Nuragus di Cagliari DOC.

grapes.name: Torbato
grapes.styles: A white grown almost only around Alghero, Tourbat in Roussillon, for a dry, mineral white and a sparkling wine.

grapes.name: Nasco
grapes.styles: A Cagliari white for sweet and dry wines with a musky, honeyed scent.

grapes.name: Malvasia di Sardegna
grapes.styles: The Malvasia of Bosa on the west coast, made dry under flor or sweet, in the same flor tradition as Vernaccia di Oristano.

law.classification: Sardinia has one DOCG, Vermentino di Gallura, a DOC since 1975 and raised in 1996 for whites of at least 95 per cent Vermentino from the granite of the north east, with a Superiore tier. The island wide DOCs are the ones a server meets: Cannonau di Sardegna (1972), at least 85 per cent Cannonau with the Classico, Capo Ferrato, Jerzu and Oliena (Nepente di Oliena) sub-zones and a Riserva after two years; Vermentino di Sardegna; Monica di Sardegna; Moscato di Sardegna. The local DOCs are Carignano del Sulcis (1977) in the south west, Vernaccia di Oristano, the island's first DOC in 1971, Malvasia di Bosa, Alghero on the north west coast, home of the Sella & Mosca estate, Mandrolisai for a Bovale, Cannonau and Monica blend of the centre, and the Cagliari family of Nuragus, Nasco, Girò, Malvasia and Moscato di Cagliari. Isola dei Nuraghi IGT covers the island and carries the famous barrique aged blends.

made.viticulture: The island's old vineyard is the alberello, the bush vine, which suits the wind and the drought: in the Sulcis the Carignano stands on its own roots in deep coastal sand that phylloxera could not cross, some of it a century old, and at Mamoiada the Cannonau grows as bush vines on granite sand at 600 to 700 metres. Newer plantings are spur pruned cordon and Guyot, and irrigation is common on the Campidano plain. The maestrale dries the canopy and keeps rot and mildew away, so spraying is light and organic farming easy; the same wind and the summer drought keep yields low without effort. Cannonau is harvested in September and reaches high sugar quickly, so growers in the mountains rely on altitude and cold nights to hold acidity. Vermentino in the Gallura is picked early to keep its bite. Vernaccia di Oristano grows on the flat alluvial gravel of the Tirso, where the vines are cropped for ripeness and the wine is left to the cellar. Co-operatives founded in the mid twentieth century still make a large share of the island's wine, Santadi, Gallura, Jerzu and Dorgali among them.
made.winemaking: Cannonau is made as a warm, soft red: a short to medium maceration, ageing in large old casks or cement for the DOC, and barrique for the Riserva and the IGT blends; the old sweet and fortified Cannonau, Anghelu Ruju among them, is made from dried grapes in the Alghero tradition. Carignano del Sulcis takes longer maceration and a year or two in oak for the Superiore and Riserva, with the Terre Brune of the Santadi co-operative, from 1984, as the model. Vermentino is cool fermented in steel and bottled young, the Gallura DOCG often with a few months on the lees for weight; a Superiore reaches thirteen per cent or more. Vernaccia di Oristano is the island's curiosity: fully fermented, then left for years in old chestnut and oak casks not filled to the top, where a film of flor yeast grows as in Jerez and gives the nutty, dry, oxidative character; the Riserva spends four years and a liquoroso version is fortified. Malvasia di Bosa is made the same way or as a sweet passito. Torbato at Alghero is made still and sparkling.

places.name: Gallura
places.note: The granite north east around Tempio Pausania and the Costa Smeralda, windy and bright, where Vermentino gives the island's only DOCG; the co-operative Cantina di Gallura and the Capichera estate of Arzachena are its names.

places.name: Nuoro, Mamoiada and the Ogliastra
places.note: The mountainous east, the Classico zone of Cannonau di Sardegna: Mamoiada's old bush vines on granite at 600 to 700 metres, Oliena's Nepente, Dorgali, and Jerzu in the Ogliastra with its own sub-zone and co-operative.

places.name: Mamoiada
places.note: A Barbagia village of masked carnival and old alberello Cannonau, whose small growers make some of the island's most structured Cannonau.

places.name: Sulcis
places.note: The south western lowlands and islands around Santadi and Sant'Antioco, where Carignano stands ungrafted in coastal sand and the Santadi co-operative's Terre Brune and Rocca Rubia set the standard; Carignano del Sulcis DOC since 1977.

places.name: Oristano and the Tirso
places.note: The west coast plain and lagoons at the mouth of the Tirso, home of Vernaccia di Oristano, the flor aged white that was Sardinia's first DOC in 1971; Cabras is the village of its reference house, Contini.

places.name: Cagliari and the Campidano
places.note: The southern capital and the hot plain behind it: Nuragus, Nasco, Monica and Malvasia under the Cagliari DOCs, and Serdiana, the village of Argiolas, maker of Turriga.

places.name: Alghero
places.note: The Catalan speaking town of the north west, with the Sella & Mosca estate founded in 1899, Torbato as its own white, the sweet Anghelu Ruju Cannonau and a Cabernet that proved the island could make it.

places.name: Bosa and the Planargia
places.note: The west coast hills above Bosa for the rare Malvasia di Bosa, dry under flor or sweet.

producers.name: Argiolas
producers.why: The Serdiana estate of 1938 whose Turriga, a Cannonau led barrique blend first made in 1988, is the island's most famous red, with Costera Cannonau and Is Argiolas Vermentino beneath it.

producers.name: Sella & Mosca
producers.why: The Alghero estate founded in 1899 by two Piedmontese, long the island's largest, with Torbato Terre Bianche, the Marchese di Villamarina Cabernet and the sweet Anghelu Ruju Cannonau.

producers.name: Attilio Contini
producers.why: The Cabras family house of 1898 whose Antico Gregori solera is the reference Vernaccia di Oristano.

producers.name: Cantina Santadi
producers.why: The Sulcis co-operative whose Terre Brune of 1984 and Rocca Rubia turned ungrafted bush vine Carignano into a serious red.

producers.name: Capichera
producers.why: The Arzachena estate in the Gallura that made Vermentino a wine of weight and ageing, with a barrel aged version, long sold outside the DOCG as IGT.

producers.name: Cantina di Gallura
producers.why: The Tempio Pausania co-operative founded in 1956 and a leading name in Vermentino di Gallura, with Canayli as its Superiore.

producers.name: Giuseppe Sedilesu
producers.why: The Mamoiada estate, named for a founder of the 1970s, that put the village's old bush vine Cannonau on the map with Mamuthone.

producers.name: Cantina Sociale di Jerzu
producers.why: The Ogliastra co-operative of 1950 behind the Jerzu sub-zone of Cannonau di Sardegna.

producers.name: Tenute Dettori
producers.why: A Sennori estate in the north working old Cannonau and Vermentino vines without additions, the island's natural wine reference.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean and dry, with hot summers and mild winters, and the maestrale, the north west wind that blows most days and keeps the vines dry and the yields down. The interior mountains of the Gennargentu bring cold nights to the Cannonau vineyards of Mamoiada and Jerzu at 400 to 700 metres; the Gallura is windy and bright; the Campidano plain in the south is the hottest ground. Drought is the yearly hazard.
terroir.soils: Granite is the island's bedrock, weathered to coarse sand in the Gallura and at Mamoiada; limestone and clay cover the Campidano and the hills around Cagliari; the Sulcis coast is deep sand where Carignano grows on its own roots; basalt plateaux, the giare, rise in the centre; Oristano's Vernaccia stands on the alluvial gravel of the Tirso.
terroir.topography: A mountainous island with the Gennargentu massif at its heart, high plateaux of basalt and granite, and one large plain, the Campidano, running from Cagliari north west to Oristano. The vineyards sit in the Gallura hills of the north east, the Nuoro and Ogliastra mountains of the east, the Sulcis lowlands of the south west and the Alghero coast of the north west.
terroir.water: The Tyrrhenian to the east and the Sardinian sea to the west; the Tirso, the island's longest river, reaches the sea at Oristano through the lagoons where the Vernaccia grows. The Strait of Bonifacio separates the Gallura from Corsica, which grows the same grape as Vermentinu.

traps: Vernaccia di Oristano is a flor aged, oxidative white of Sardinia; Vernaccia di San Gimignano is a fresh Tuscan white from a different grape.
Cannonau and Grenache are one variety, whichever shore it began on; local pride argues for Sardinia, and the exam wants only the identity.
Vermentino di Gallura is the DOCG; Vermentino di Sardegna is the DOC. Both are Vermentino, and only Gallura is granite.
Carignano del Sulcis is Carignan and often better than the French reputation; do not dismiss it as a blending grape here.
Malvasia di Bosa and Vernaccia di Oristano are both flor aged; Malvasia is the west coast's, Vernaccia the Tirso plain's.
Sardinia lies west of the mainland and south of Corsica; it is not off the toe of Italy, which is Sicily's place.
Nepente di Oliena is a sub-zone of Cannonau di Sardegna, not a separate grape.

wines.note: Red cherry, dried herbs, leather and warmth at fourteen per cent and more, with soft tannin; the Riserva waits two years and the mountain villages of Mamoiada and Jerzu give the most structure. Roast suckling pig, lamb, pecorino sardo.

The DOCG from the granite of the north east: fuller and more saline than other Vermentino, with citrus, white peach, wild herbs and a bitter almond finish; the Superiore carries more alcohol. Grilled fish, bottarga, lobster from the Gallura coast.
The lighter island wide DOC, fresh, lemony and herbal, the everyday white with fregola, clams and sea urchin.

Dark, smooth and savoury from old bush vines on sand, plum and Mediterranean scrub with soft tannin; the Superiore and Riserva from the Santadi co-operative age for a decade. Lamb stew, wild boar, malloreddus with sausage.

A dry, amber, flor aged white of walnut, almond and bitter orange at fifteen per cent or more, aged for years in old casks; the Riserva and the fortified liquoroso are the deepest. An aperitivo with bottarga, or with almond pastries.
The island's famous blend, Cannonau led with Carignano, Bovale and Malvasia Nera, aged in barrique: rich, dark and long lived, the wine that showed Sardinia could make a world class red in the 1980s.
A rare golden wine from the Planargia coast, dry under flor or sweet and raisined, with apricot, honey and bitter almond; served with seadas, the honeyed cheese fritters.

exam: Etna: DOC 1968, the island's first; Rosso at least 80 per cent Nerello Mascalese, Bianco at least 60 per cent Carricante, Bianco Superiore from Milo at 80; contrade as crus; DOCG applied for in 2023 and pending.
Cerasuolo di Vittoria is Sicily's only DOCG (2005): Nero d'Avola 50 to 70 with Frappato 30 to 50; a red, not a rosato.

Marsala's grades by age (Fine 1, Superiore 2, Superiore Riserva 4, Vergine 5, Stravecchio 10), colour (Oro, Ambra, Rubino) and sugar (Secco, Semisecco, Dolce); Vergine is dry and refuses cooked must and mistella; 1773 and John Woodhouse.
Nero d'Avola is Calabrese; Avola is a town; varietal Nero d'Avola and Grillo must be Sicilia DOC since 2017.
Grillo is Catarratto crossed with Zibibbo; Zibibbo is Muscat of Alexandria; Pantelleria dries it for passito.
Nerello Mascalese tastes like a mountain Pinot or Nebbiolo: pale, high acid, fine tannin, ash; do not call it a big southern red.
The geography: Etna's north, east and south faces, Vittoria's sand, Trapani's sea of vines, Pantelleria near Tunisia, the Aeolians.
The producers that remade the island: Regaleali 1970, Planeta 1995, Benanti 1988, Terre Nere and Passopisciaro in the 2000s, De Bartoli 1978.

grapes.name: Nero d'Avola
grapes.styles: Calabrese by its old name, the island's most planted red: dark plum and black cherry with soft, round tannin from the warm west and the south east, and a firmer, more aromatic wine from Pachino and Noto near the sea; the major part of Cerasuolo di Vittoria.

grapes.name: Nerello Mascalese
grapes.styles: Etna's red, named for the plain of Mascali: pale ruby, red cherry, dried herbs, smoke and ash over high acid and fine, firm tannin, closer to Nebbiolo or a mountain Pinot Noir than to anything else on the island.

grapes.name: Nerello Cappuccio
grapes.styles: The darker, softer partner of Nerello Mascalese on Etna, allowed to a fifth of Etna Rosso for colour and flesh.

grapes.name: Carricante
grapes.styles: Etna's white, high in acid, lemon, green apple and a saline, flinty edge, most at home on the rainy east face at Milo where Etna Bianco Superiore is made; it ages like a Riesling.

grapes.name: Frappato
grapes.styles: The perfumed, pale, strawberry scented red of Vittoria, light in tannin, which lifts Nero d'Avola in Cerasuolo di Vittoria and is bottled alone, often chilled.

grapes.name: Grillo
grapes.styles: A cross of Catarratto and Zibibbo, the backbone of fine Marsala and now the island's best dry white: citrus, herbs and a saline bite, reserved to Sicilia DOC as a varietal since 2017.

grapes.name: Catarratto
grapes.styles: Long the most planted grape of Sicily, a neutral white of the west that fed Marsala and the bulk trade; fresh and lemony from the hills at low yields.

grapes.name: Inzolia
grapes.styles: Ansonica on the mainland: a soft, nutty white of the west, a partner in Marsala and in dry blends with Grillo and Catarratto.

grapes.name: Zibibbo
grapes.styles: Muscat of Alexandria on Pantelleria, grown as low bush vines in hollows against the wind and sun dried for Passito di Pantelleria; also a dry aromatic white.

grapes.name: Malvasia di Lipari
grapes.styles: The Aeolian islands' Malvasia, dried for the apricot and honey sweet wine of Malvasia delle Lipari with a little Corinto Nero.

grapes.name: Perricone
grapes.styles: Pignatello, the old red of the west, for Rubino Marsala and a few varietal reds.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: The international red that suits the warm interior best, grown around Menfi and Sclafani since the 1990s.

law.classification: Sicily has one DOCG, Cerasuolo di Vittoria, promoted in 2005 for a Nero d'Avola and Frappato blend from the south east with a Classico zone. Etna, the island's first DOC in 1968, carries Rosso, Bianco, Bianco Superiore from Milo, Rosato and Spumante and lets growers print one of the named contrade; its consortium voted in November 2023 to seek DOCG, and no promotion had been published at the time of writing. Marsala DOC (1969) is a fortified wine with grades by age, colour and sweetness. Sicilia DOC, created in 2011 to replace the island wide IGT, has reserved varietal Grillo and Nero d'Avola to itself since the 2017 vintage, with Terre Siciliane IGT beneath it for everything else. The other DOCs are many: Moscato and Passito di Pantelleria, Malvasia delle Lipari, Faro near Messina, Vittoria, Eloro and Noto in the south east, Alcamo, Menfi, Contessa Entellina, Contea di Sclafani, Monreale, Sambuca di Sicilia and Mamertino among them.

made.viticulture: Two vineyards share the island. The west, Trapani province, is a sea of Catarratto, Grillo and Inzolia on spur pruned cordon and the old alberello, cropped for Marsala and the bulk trade and now also for dry whites. Etna is the opposite: dry stone terraces of black lava on the north, east and south faces from 400 to over 1,000 metres, old alberello Nerello Mascalese vines on their own roots in the volcanic sand, and some of the latest harvests in Italy, with Carricante highest on the rainy east face at Milo. The slopes are divided into contrade, named districts on lava flows of different ages, bottled like crus. In the south east, Vittoria's Frappato and Nero d'Avola grow on red sand with sea breezes, and Pachino and Noto give Nero d'Avola on white limestone by the sea. On Pantelleria, Zibibbo is grown as the alberello pantesco, a bush vine pruned into a hollow dug against the wind, a method listed by UNESCO in 2014. The dry air keeps rot away, so most serious estates farm organically; the hazards are drought, the scirocco and the volcano itself.
made.winemaking: Etna Rosso is made as a mountain red: gentle extraction, often whole bunches or part of them, and ageing in large old casks or used barrique so that the ash and herb of Nerello Mascalese are not covered; Etna Bianco is cool fermented and held on lees, the Superiore of Milo sometimes in old wood for years. Cerasuolo di Vittoria is fermented warm and briefly for freshness, some of it in amphorae by the estates that revived the DOCG. Marsala is the island's old craft: a base of Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia fortified with grape spirit and, below Vergine, sweetened with mistella (must stopped with alcohol, the sifone), with mosto cotto (cooked must) allowed only in the Ambra colour, then aged oxidatively in cask for one to ten years by grade, the Vergine often in a solera. Pantelleria's passito is made by drying Zibibbo in the sun for weeks and adding the raisins to fermenting fresh must; the Aeolian Malvasia is dried the same way.

places.name: Etna
places.note: The volcano on the east coast whose DOC arcs around its north, east and south faces from Randazzo to Santa Maria di Licodia, leaving out the west; old ungrafted Nerello Mascalese on terraces of black lava, Carricante on the wet east face, and contrade named like crus; a revival from 1988 and the arrival of mainland and foreign estates in the 2000s made it the island's most prized zone.

places.name: The north slope, Randazzo to Linguaglossa
places.note: Castiglione di Sicilia's villages of Passopisciaro, Solicchiata and Rovittello and the contrade Calderara, Feudo di Mezzo, Guardiola, Rampante, Arcurìa, Santo Spirito and Sciaranuova: the heart of Etna Rosso, cool and late harvested.

places.name: Milo and the east slope
places.note: The rainy east face above Giarre where Carricante is most at home and Etna Bianco Superiore is permitted from Milo alone.

places.name: The south east slope
places.note: Viagrande, Trecastagni and Santa Venerina above Catania, warmer and lower, where Benanti began.

places.name: Vittoria and the south east
places.note: Red sand over limestone with sea breezes in the Ragusa province, home of the Cerasuolo di Vittoria DOCG and of Frappato; the natural wine estates of the 1980s and 2000s revived it, one of them in amphorae.

places.name: Noto, Eloro and Pachino
places.note: The south eastern tip around Syracuse: Nero d'Avola at its most structured on white limestone by the sea at Pachino, Eloro DOC with its Pachino sub-zone, and Moscato di Noto. Avola, the grape's namesake, is a town rather than an appellation.

places.name: Marsala and the west
places.note: Trapani province, the island's largest vineyard, warm and low: the Marsala DOC around the port where the British trade began in 1773, and the dry Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia whites of Alcamo and the south west that grew out of it.

places.name: Menfi and Contessa Entellina
places.note: Two DOCs of the south west coast and hills that carry the island's largest modern estates, with Chardonnay, Syrah and Nero d'Avola beside the native whites.

places.name: The interior: Contea di Sclafani
places.note: High hills in the centre of the island around the Regaleali estate, a DOC where altitude cools Nero d'Avola, Perricone and Catarratto; the home of Rosso del Conte of 1970.

places.name: Pantelleria
places.note: A volcanic island closer to Tunisia than to Sicily, arid and wind blasted, where Zibibbo grows in hollows as the alberello pantesco and dries in the sun for Passito di Pantelleria; Ben Ryé is its famous bottle.

places.name: The Aeolian islands and Faro
places.note: Lipari and Salina off the north east coast for Malvasia delle Lipari, and Faro DOC on the hills above Messina for Nerello Mascalese led reds, Etna's cousins.

producers.name: Tasca d'Almerita
producers.why: The Regaleali estate in the interior since 1830, whose Rosso del Conte of 1970 was an early benchmark for Nero d'Avola; now also on Etna (Tascante), Salina and Mozia.

producers.name: Donnafugata
producers.why: A Marsala family's house of 1983 with estates at Contessa Entellina, on Etna and on Pantelleria, where Ben Ryé is the reference Passito di Pantelleria.

producers.name: Planeta
producers.why: The 1995 estate that put modern Sicily on the world's lists with Chardonnay and Nero d'Avola from Menfi, then Cerasuolo di Vittoria, Noto and Etna.

producers.name: Benanti
producers.why: The Viagrande house whose revival of Etna from 1988, with the Pietra Marina Etna Bianco Superiore from Milo and Rovittello Rosso, proved the volcano.

producers.name: Tenuta delle Terre Nere
producers.why: A north slope estate of 2002 that made contrada bottlings the Etna habit, with a prephylloxera plot in Calderara Sottana.

producers.name: Passopisciaro
producers.why: The north slope estate founded in 2000 by the maker of Tuscany's Tenuta di Trinoro, whose single contrada Nerello Mascalese bottlings, named by their lava flows, set the cru idea on Etna.

producers.name: Graci
producers.why: A Passopisciaro family estate in large old casks, with Arcurìa and the high Barbabecchi plot as its contrade.

producers.name: Girolamo Russo
producers.why: A north slope estate at Passopisciaro named for the founder's father, with Feudo, San Lorenzo and Feudo di Mezzo as its contrada Etna Rosso.

producers.name: Cornelissen
producers.why: The Belgian born natural winemaker of Solicchiata on the north slope, sold under his full name, whose Magma is a cult wine of the natural movement.

producers.name: COS
producers.why: The Vittoria estate of 1980 that revived Cerasuolo di Vittoria and ferments it in buried amphorae.

producers.name: Occhipinti
producers.why: A Vittoria grower sold under her full name whose Il Frappato and SP68 wines made the grape a natural wine standard.

producers.name: Marco De Bartoli
producers.why: The Marsala estate founded in 1978 by a man who died in 2011, whose unfortified Vecchio Samperi solera and Marsala Superiore restored the wine's honour, with Zibibbo on Pantelleria.

producers.name: Florio
producers.why: The Marsala house founded in 1833 by a Palermo merchant family beside the British firms, still the city's great cellar for Superiore Riserva and Vergine.

producers.name: Gulfi
producers.why: A Chiaramonte Gulfi estate with single vineyard Nero d'Avola from Pachino's limestone, the grape's best case for terroir.

terroir.climate: Hot, dry, bright Mediterranean, with the scirocco off Africa and almost no summer rain, so disease pressure is low and organic farming common. Altitude and the sea are the correctives: Etna has snow in winter, rain on its east face, cold nights and a harvest that runs into late October and November for Nerello Mascalese, among the latest in Italy, while the high interior hills of Sclafani and the south east coast's breezes do the same work lower down. Pantelleria is windswept and arid.
terroir.soils: Etna's slopes are volcanic ash, lapilli, pumice and broken basalt of different ages, each lava flow its own soil, which is why the contrade differ. Vittoria and the south east lie on red sand over limestone; the west and the interior are calcareous clay, marl and sand; Pantelleria and the Aeolian islands are volcanic again; Noto and Pachino are white limestone and sand near the sea.
terroir.topography: A triangle of mountains and hills: Etna at over 3,300 metres in the east, the Peloritani and Madonie ranges along the north coast, the Iblei plateau in the south east, and the rolling western hills of Trapani province, the island's largest vineyard area. Vineyards pass 1,000 metres on Etna; the Marsala country is low and warm.
terroir.water: The Tyrrhenian to the north, the Ionian to the east and the Strait of Sicily to the south, with Tunisia some seventy kilometres from Pantelleria. Rivers are seasonal; the sea breezes at Vittoria, Pachino and Menfi and the snowmelt on Etna matter more than any stream.

traps: Cerasuolo di Vittoria is a red DOCG blend; Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosato. The word means cherry coloured in both and the wines share nothing else.
Etna was still a DOC at the time of writing, whatever the trade press anticipated; until a DOCG decree appears, Cerasuolo di Vittoria is the island's only DOCG.
Nero d'Avola is a grape; Avola is a town in the south east, not an appellation.
Marsala Vergine is dry by definition; Marsala Fine is the cooking grade; neither is the sweet Marsala a guest may expect.
Nerello Mascalese is not Nero d'Avola, and Etna Rosso is a different wine from Sicilia DOC Nero d'Avola.
Grillo is a native cross, not an import; Inzolia and Ansonica are one grape.
Zibibbo is Muscat of Alexandria, not Moscato Bianco; Moscato di Noto is the Bianco.
Terre Siciliane IGT may not carry varietal Grillo or Nero d'Avola since 2017; those two words mean Sicilia DOC.

wines.note: Nerello Mascalese with up to a fifth of Nerello Cappuccio: pale, scented, taut and ashy, with red cherry, dried herbs and fine tannin; a contrada on the label names the district. Serve a shade cool with lamb, mushrooms or tuna; it decants like a Nebbiolo.

Carricante, lemon, green apple and flint with piercing acidity and a saline finish; the Superiore, from Milo alone, at least 80 per cent Carricante, ages for a decade. Raw fish, grilled swordfish, pasta with bottarga.
Nero d'Avola with 30 to 50 per cent Frappato: medium ruby, cherry, strawberry and spice, soft tannin and lift, the island's first DOCG. Serve lightly cool with tuna, caponata and spiced pork.

Dark, plummy and warm with black cherry and liquorice, soft in the west and more structured from Pachino and Noto; sold as Sicilia DOC. Grilled meats, sausage with fennel, aubergine and tomato dishes.
Dry, citrus and herb scented with a saline grip and a little weight, the island's best varietal white and a Sicilia DOC wine by rule; sardines, pasta con le sarde, fried seafood.

Grillo, Catarratto and Inzolia, fortified and oxidatively aged four years: amber, dried fig, walnut and caramel, sweet or dry; the cooking Marsala of the supermarket is the Fine grade and a different thing. Serve with aged pecorino, almond pastries or alone.

The dry grade by definition, five years in cask and often a solera, with no cooked must or mistella allowed: nutty, saline and bone dry, the Sicilian answer to amontillado. An aperitivo or a wine for salted almonds and anchovies.

Zibibbo sun dried on the island between Sicily and Tunisia, then added to fermenting fresh must: amber, apricot, orange peel and honey with a saline edge. Pour it with cassata, blue cheese or dark chocolate.
The Aeolian islands' dried Malvasia with a touch of Corinto Nero: golden, apricot and honey, lighter than Pantelleria's wine; almond biscuits and ricotta desserts.

exam: Name the three native reds and where each lives: Schiava (Santa Maddalena, Lago di Caldaro), Lagrein (Bolzano, Gries), Teroldego (Campo Rotaliano).
Trento DOC: created 1993, traditional method only, Chardonnay and Pinot Nero, 15, 24 and 36 months on the lees.
Read a German-language label: Vernatsch, Weissburgunder, Grauburgunder, Blauburgunder, Kretzer, Südtirol.
Gewürztraminer's home village is Tramin (Termeno); the exam asks it as geography, not as style.
Why the whites are so precise: altitude, the day to night swing, porphyry and limestone, co-operative scale over tiny holdings.
Vino Santo Trentino is Nosiola; Vin Santo is Tuscany; the exam likes the one-letter difference.
Delle Venezie DOC (2017) covers Pinot Grigio across Veneto, Friuli and Trentino, not Alto Adige.
The 2024 change: eighty-six UGAs for Alto Adige DOC, recognised by the ministry in 2024.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Among Alto Adige's most planted grapes and the proof that the variety can be serious: dry, full, pear and smoke, with real acidity from altitude.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Tramin, Termeno in Italian, is the village the grape is named for; Alto Adige makes it dry, oily and rose scented, often at fourteen per cent.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder on a German label; the Terlano blends and single sites age for decades on porphyry, which few Pinot Biancos anywhere do.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Taut and grassy from the cooler slopes; a part of the Terlano cuvée and a varietal wine of growing reputation.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: The backbone of Trento DOC and of its reserve cuvées; still versions are made in both provinces.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Pinot Nero, or Blauburgunder, gives Trento DOC its rosé and its structure, and makes a fine varietal red on the Mazzon terrace above Egna.

grapes.name: Schiava
grapes.styles: Vernatsch in German; the pale, soft, strawberry and bitter almond red of Santa Maddalena and Lago di Caldaro, drunk young and lightly chilled.

grapes.name: Lagrein
grapes.styles: Bolzano's own dark grape, from the Gries district: deep colour, plum and chocolate, firm tannin, made as Dunkel (dark) or Kretzer (rosé).

grapes.name: Teroldego
grapes.styles: Trentino's native red from the gravel of the Campo Rotaliano: deep violet, blackberry and tar, bright acid, modest tannin.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Thrives at the highest sites of Alto Adige and the Cembra valley, where it keeps the acidity it loses on Germany's warm plains.

grapes.name: Kerner
grapes.styles: A Riesling and Schiava Grossa cross from 1929 that gives sharp, peachy whites in the Valle Isarco.

grapes.name: Marzemino
grapes.styles: Trentino's soft, violet scented red from Isera in the Vallagarina, praised in a line of Mozart's Don Giovanni.

grapes.name: Nosiola
grapes.styles: Trentino's only native white, from the Valle dei Laghi; dried on racks for the rare, amber Vino Santo Trentino.

law.classification: Both provinces work under the national ladder of DOCG, DOC and IGT, but neither holds a DOCG; the region's reputation rests on its DOCs. Alto Adige DOC, Südtirol on a German label, covers almost all of the province's wine, the highest DOC share in Italy, and carries sub-zone names: Valle Isarco, Val Venosta, Terlano, Santa Maddalena, Colli di Bolzano and Meranese. Lago di Caldaro DOC, a Schiava wine, is shared with Trentino. In 2024 the ministry recognised eighty-six Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive for Alto Adige DOC, named sites with yields cut by a quarter and a short list of permitted grapes, usable from the 2024 vintage. Trentino DOC is the province-wide varietal DOC, with Trentino Superiore for stricter wines; Teroldego Rotaliano DOC is the native red's own appellation; Trento DOC, created in 1993, was Italy's first DOC written solely for traditional method sparkling wine and is sold under the collective name Trentodoc. Pinot Grigio from Trentino may also be sold under the three-region delle Venezie DOC, created in 2017. Vigneti delle Dolomiti IGT covers the rest.
labels: the same grape on a German or Italian label
the same grape; Grauburgunder or Ruländer is Pinot Grigio, Blauburgunder is Pinot Nero
longer ageing; for Trento DOC, 36 months on the lees
a vintage sparkling wine; for Trento DOC, at least 24 months on the lees

Trentino's Nosiola passito; Vin Santo is the Tuscan wine

tiers: Alto Adige DOC (Südtirol)
One province-wide DOC with sub-zones; a varietal name on the label means at least 85 per cent of that grape, printed in Italian and German.
Alto Adige sub-zones
Valle Isarco, Val Venosta, Terlano, Santa Maddalena, Colli di Bolzano and Meranese follow the DOC name; Lago di Caldaro is a separate DOC shared with Trentino.
UGA (Unità Geografica Aggiuntiva)
Eighty-six named sites recognised by the ministry in 2024, each with a yield cut of a quarter and at most five permitted grapes, every grape grown inside the site; the first vintage is 2024.
Trento DOC
Traditional method only, from Chardonnay, Pinot Nero, Pinot Bianco and Pinot Meunier: 15 months on the lees for non-vintage, 24 for a vintage wine, 36 for a riserva.
Trentino DOC and Trentino Superiore
The province's varietal DOC; Superiore wines carry lower yields and a higher minimum alcohol.
Teroldego Rotaliano DOC
The Campo Rotaliano's own appellation for Teroldego, as rosso, rosato (Kretzer) and Superiore Riserva.
Delle Venezie DOC
Since 2017 the three-region Pinot Grigio DOC for Veneto, Friuli Venezia Giulia and the province of Trento; Alto Adige is outside it.
Vigneti delle Dolomiti IGT
The broad regional IGT for both provinces, Weinberg Dolomiten in German.

made.viticulture: The old training here is the pergola, a tilted overhead trellis that shades Schiava and Teroldego from the hot valley floor and lets air through the fruit; Guyot and other vertical systems have replaced most of it on the hillsides since the 1980s, but the pergola trentina still covers the Campo Rotaliano. Vineyards sit on terraces held by dry stone walls in the Valle Isarco and the Cembra valley, so the work is by hand. Growers match grape to altitude and aspect with unusual care: Lagrein and Cabernet on the warm basin floor, Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon and Chardonnay in the middle, Riesling, Kerner, Sylvaner and Müller-Thurgau highest. Co-operatives founded around the turn of the last century, Terlano in 1893, Tramin in 1898 and San Michele Appiano in 1907, still take in most of Alto Adige's fruit from thousands of tiny holdings, which keeps quality even across the province. Harvest runs from late August for sparkling base wine to October for Lagrein and late picked Gewürztraminer. The hazards are spring frost at altitude, hail in summer and rot in a wet autumn.
made.winemaking: The whites are made cleanly and reductively: cool fermentation in steel, a few months on the fine lees and early bottling to hold aroma, though Chardonnay, Pinot Bianco and the Terlano cuvées are often part fermented in large old oak and the reserve bottlings are held on lees for years. Gewürztraminer is picked ripe and fermented dry to full weight. Schiava is fermented briefly so that colour and tannin stay light, and bottled early. Lagrein takes a longer maceration and time in barrel for the Riserva, or is drawn off pink after a short contact for Kretzer. Teroldego is handled like a mid weight red in cement and large oak, and at one estate in clay amphorae. Trento DOC follows the traditional method: second fermentation in bottle, a minimum of fifteen months on the lees for non-vintage wines, twenty-four for a vintage and thirty-six for a riserva. Vino Santo Trentino dries Nosiola on arele racks for months, ferments it very slowly and ages it in small casks for years.

places.name: Alto Adige (Südtirol)
places.note: The northern province around Bolzano, Austrian until 1919 and officially bilingual today; once a Schiava red country, now mostly white, almost all of it DOC and most of it made by a dozen co-operatives of rare quality.

places.name: Bolzano (Bozen) and Santa Maddalena
places.note: The warm basin where the Isarco meets the Adige. Santa Maddalena (St. Magdalener) on the porphyry hill above the town is the classic Schiava sub-zone of Alto Adige DOC, at least 85 per cent Schiava with Lagrein allowed to deepen it; Gries, across the river, is Lagrein's historic home around the Muri-Gries monastery.

places.name: Terlano (Terlan)
places.note: Northwest of Bolzano on quartz porphyry: Pinot Bianco, Sauvignon and Chardonnay of unusual length and ageing power, made famous by the village co-operative founded in 1893 and its reserve wines held for years on the lees.

places.name: Oltradige (Überetsch): Appiano and Caldaro
places.note: The hills west of the Adige: Lago di Caldaro (Kalterersee) DOC for light Schiava, and the Appiano villages for Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay and Sauvignon on limestone rubble.

places.name: Bassa Atesina (Unterland): Termeno, Magrè, Cortaccia, Egna
places.note: The southern stretch of the valley: Tramin (Termeno) for Gewürztraminer, the limestone slopes of Magrè and Cortaccia for Lagrein, Merlot and Cabernet, and the high Mazzon terrace above Egna for Pinot Nero.

places.name: Valle Isarco (Eisacktal)
places.note: The northeastern side valley towards the Brenner: the highest, coolest zone, on schist and moraine, for Sylvaner, Kerner, Müller-Thurgau, Riesling and Grüner Veltliner; the Augustinian abbey of Novacella (Neustift), founded in 1142, is its landmark cellar.

places.name: Val Venosta (Vinschgau)
places.note: The dry western valley towards Merano and the Swiss border, apple country with a few high, steep Riesling and Pinot Nero sites on glacial slopes.

places.name: Trentino
places.note: The southern province around Trento, Italian speaking, warmer and lower, with the valley floor given to Pinot Grigio, Chardonnay and Müller-Thurgau in volume and the side valleys to its native grapes.

places.name: Trento DOC
places.note: The sparkling appellation, drawn on the hillside vineyards of the whole province, some near 800 metres; Chardonnay leads, with Pinot Nero for rosé and structure, and the long lees minimums are the law's whole point. Ferrari, founded in Trento in 1902, is the house that built it.

places.name: Campo Rotaliano
places.note: The gravel plain north of Trento where the Noce meets the Adige, between Mezzolombardo and Mezzocorona: Teroldego's only serious home, under Teroldego Rotaliano DOC.

places.name: Valle di Cembra
places.note: A steep porphyry valley of dry stone terraces northeast of Trento: Müller-Thurgau and sparkling base wine from some of the region's highest vines.

places.name: Vallagarina and Isera
places.note: The Adige valley south of Trento towards Rovereto: Marzemino on the basalt of Isera and the Ziresi vineyard, Trentino's soft, floral red.

places.name: Valle dei Laghi
places.note: The small lake valley west of Trento where Nosiola is grown and dried for Vino Santo Trentino.

producers.name: Ferrari
producers.why: Founded in Trento in 1902 and the house that made Trento DOC; its Giulio Ferrari Riserva del Fondatore, a Chardonnay held about a decade on the lees, is Italy's reference sparkling wine.

producers.name: Cesarini Sforza
producers.why: A Trento DOC house founded in 1974, known for Brut and Rosé at a fair price and a good way to pour Trentodoc by the glass.

producers.name: Foradori
producers.why: The Campo Rotaliano estate that rescued Teroldego from bulk production with low yields, massal selection, biodynamics and clay amphorae.

producers.name: Cantina Terlano
producers.why: The 1893 co-operative whose Pinot Bianco, Terlaner cuvée and Rarity bottlings are the proof that Alto Adige whites age for decades.

producers.name: Cantina Tramin
producers.why: The co-operative of the village that gave Gewürztraminer its name; its Nussbaumer is the grape's Italian benchmark.

producers.name: Alois Lageder
producers.why: A Magrè house founded in 1823, biodynamic, with single site Pinot Bianco, Chardonnay and Lagrein that set the modern standard for the Bassa Atesina.

producers.name: Abbazia di Novacella
producers.why: An Augustinian abbey in the Valle Isarco, founded in 1142, and the reference for Sylvaner, Kerner and Riesling from the high north.

producers.name: J. Hofstätter
producers.why: A Tramin estate founded in 1907 whose Pinot Nero from the Mazzon terrace is the variety's Italian standard bearer, with Gewürztraminer from the village itself.

producers.name: San Michele Appiano
producers.why: The 1907 co-operative of the Oltradige whose Sanct Valentin range of Sauvignon and Pinot Bianco pushed co-operative wine into the top tier.

producers.name: Cantina Bolzano
producers.why: The city co-operative that holds Santa Maddalena and Gries Lagrein, the two native reds of the basin.

producers.name: Mezzacorona
producers.why: Trentino's large co-operative on the Campo Rotaliano, the volume source for Pinot Grigio and Teroldego, with Rotari as its Trento DOC label.

producers.name: Cavit
producers.why: The federation of Trentino co-operatives and the province's biggest producer, with Altemasi as its Trento DOC label.

terroir.climate: Alpine continental. The Alps block the north wind and the valley floor around Bolzano traps summer heat, so the basin ripens Lagrein and even Cabernet while sites a few hundred metres higher stay cool enough for Riesling and Kerner. Nights fall sharply at every altitude, which is what keeps the whites aromatic and the acids firm. The Ora, an afternoon wind that climbs the valley from Lake Garda, dries the Trentino vineyards after summer storms. Hail and spring frost are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Porphyry, a reddish volcanic rock, underlies Bolzano, Terlano and Santa Maddalena and is credited with the long life of the Terlano whites. The Isarco valley works schist, phyllite and glacial moraine; the Oltradige hills and the Bassa Atesina sit on limestone and dolomite rubble over clay. Trentino's Campo Rotaliano is a flat fan of gravel and sand laid down where the Noce meets the Adige, and the Cembra valley is porphyry terrace again.
terroir.topography: A single deep trench, the Adige valley, runs north to south with the Dolomites to the east and the Ortles group to the west. Vineyards climb the valley sides from roughly 200 metres on the floor to around 1,000 metres in the Val Venosta and the Valle Isarco, on terraces held by dry stone walls. Aspect decides the grape: south and west slopes take the reds, cooler east faces and the high side valleys take the whites.
terroir.water: The Adige, Italy's second longest river, is the spine; the Isarco joins it at Bolzano and the Noce at the Campo Rotaliano. Lake Caldaro, small and warm, moderates the Oltradige and lends its name to a Schiava DOC. Lake Garda, whose northern shore is Trentino's, reaches the Adige valley as the Ora wind rather than as water.

traps: Alto Adige and Südtirol are one place with two names; Trentino is the other province, not a synonym.
Trento DOC is traditional method and Prosecco is tank method; Trentodoc is the brand name of the DOC, not a different wine.
Lagrein Kretzer is a rosé and Lagrein Dunkel is the dark red; Kretzer is not a grape.
Kerner is a Riesling cross grown in the Valle Isarco; it is not a village or a style of Riesling.
Teroldego grows on a flat gravel plain, the Campo Rotaliano, not on a hillside; the exam likes the exception.
Schiava is pale, soft and low in tannin; Schiava Grossa is the Trollinger of Württemberg under an Italian name, never a big red.
No DOCG exists in either province; the region's rank rests on its DOC share, the highest in Italy.

wines.note: Chardonnay led and bottle fermented: at least fifteen months on the lees for a non-vintage wine, two years for a vintage, three for a riserva. Mountain acidity gives a crisp line that reads leaner than Franciacorta. Pour it with fried food, oysters or as the aperitivo.
Dry, mid to full weight, pear and white peach with a saline finish; the benchmark against which the bulk Pinot Grigio of the plains is judged. Trout, risotto and antipasti.
Rose petal, lychee and ginger, dry and full, low in acid and often fourteen per cent alcohol. Spiced dishes and washed rind cheeses suit it better than fish does.
Taut, stony and slow to open; the Terlano co-operative's reserve bottlings prove that Pinot Bianco can age for decades on porphyry. Pair with white asparagus, veal and mountain cheese.
Pale ruby, strawberry, bitter almond and violets, light tannin; served cool with speck, dumplings and sausages. It is the local lunch wine, not a cellar wine.
Inky, plummy and firm with a bitter chocolate edge, softened by time in oak; Bolzano's answer to Syrah. Braised beef, game and smoked meats.
Deep violet, wild berry and tar with bright acidity and soft tannin from the gravel plain; juicy when young, serious from low yields. Serve with polenta, game birds and hard cheeses.
Nosiola dried on racks until Holy Week, then slowly fermented into a rare amber dessert wine of apricot, nuts and tremendous acidity. Vino, not Vin, separates it from the Tuscan wine.

exam: Chianti Classico: 80 per cent Sangiovese minimum, no white grapes since 2006, Riserva 24 months, Gran Selezione 30 months from estate fruit, black rooster; its own DOCG since 1996.
Brunello: 100 per cent Sangiovese, two years in oak, release in the fifth year after harvest, the sixth for Riserva; Rosso di Montalcino the year after harvest.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile) from a Tuscan town; Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is a grape; the single most tested Italian trap.

Super Tuscans by name and type: Sassicaia (Cabernet, Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC), Tignanello (Sangiovese with Cabernet), Solaia (Cabernet led), Ornellaia (Bolgheri Superiore), Masseto (Merlot), Le Pergole Torte, Cepparello and Flaccianello (pure Sangiovese IGT).

The dates: 1716 Medici decree, 1872 Ricasoli formula, 1924 consortium, 1966 the first DOCs, Vernaccia and Brunello among them, 1980 Brunello and Vino Nobile DOCG, 1992 IGT, 1996 Chianti Classico DOCG, 2013 Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC.
Soils as words: galestro and alberese; the exam asks which is the limestone (alberese).
What changed since 2020: Gran Selezione to 90 per cent Sangiovese from the 2027 vintage with eleven UGA names; Vino Nobile's Pieve tier, first released in 2025.
Vin Santo: Trebbiano and Malvasia, caratelli, the madre; Occhio di Pernice from Sangiovese; served with cantucci.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: High acid, firm tannin, sour cherry, dried herb and leather, middling colour; called Brunello at Montalcino, Prugnolo Gentile at Montepulciano and Morellino at Scansano.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: The grape of Bolgheri and of Sassicaia; a permitted partner up to 20 per cent in Chianti Classico and a required 10 to 20 per cent in Carmignano.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Bolgheri's softer half and the whole of Masseto; also a partner in Chianti Classico and the Maremma.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Adds perfume and lift to Bolgheri reds and to the Sassicaia blend; Paleo at Le Macchiole is the pure version.

grapes.name: Canaiolo
grapes.styles: The traditional softener of Chianti, named in the Ricasoli formula of 1872; now a minor partner.

grapes.name: Colorino
grapes.styles: A deeply coloured native used in small amounts to deepen Sangiovese.

grapes.name: Vernaccia
grapes.styles: San Gimignano's dry, nutty, faintly bitter white, a DOC in 1966 among Italy's first, and Tuscany's only white DOCG.

grapes.name: Trebbiano
grapes.styles: Trebbiano Toscano, neutral and high in acid; with Malvasia it is dried for Vin Santo, and it was once blended into Chianti.

grapes.name: Malvasia
grapes.styles: Malvasia Bianca Lunga, the aromatic half of Vin Santo.

grapes.name: Vermentino
grapes.styles: The fresh coastal white of the Maremma and Bolgheri, herbal and saline.

grapes.name: Muscat Blanc
grapes.styles: Moscato Bianco makes Moscadello di Montalcino, a sweet or late harvest white from Brunello's hill.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: Grows well at Cortona and on the coast, and is a permitted partner in Bolgheri Rosso.

law.classification: As of 2026 Tuscany holds eleven DOCGs: Chianti, Chianti Classico, Brunello di Montalcino, Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, Carmignano, Vernaccia di San Gimignano, Morellino di Scansano, Montecucco Sangiovese, Suvereto, Rosso della Val di Cornia and Elba Aleatico Passito. Chianti Classico has been its own DOCG since 1996, separate from Chianti DOCG and its seven sub-zones, and climbs Annata, Riserva and Gran Selezione; a consortium vote of 2021 raises Gran Selezione to 90 per cent Sangiovese with native partners only from the 2027 vintage and prints eleven Unità Geografiche Aggiuntive on its labels. Montalcino stacks Brunello DOCG over the Rosso, Moscadello and Sant'Antimo DOCs. Montepulciano's Pieve tier above Riserva, approved by the ministry in 2024 and published in 2025, released its first wines, from the 2021 vintage, that year. Bolgheri DOC covers the coast, with Bolgheri Sassicaia a single estate DOC since 2013. Toscana IGT, created under the IGT law of 1992, is where the Super Tuscans live.
labels: the historic heart of a zone; in Tuscany Chianti Classico is a separate DOCG, not a sub-zone of Chianti
longer ageing set by each DOCG: 24 months for Chianti Classico, three years for Vino Nobile, the sixth year for Brunello
higher minimum alcohol and lower yields; Chianti Superiore, Bolgheri Superiore
Chianti Classico's top tier from the 2010 vintage: 30 months, estate fruit, 90 per cent Sangiovese from 2027
the black rooster of the Chianti Classico consortium, founded in 1924, on every bottle's neck
Unità Geografica Aggiuntiva, a named village zone printed on Gran Selezione labels
Montepulciano's top tier, named for a parish zone, with its first wines released in 2025
a registered single vineyard named on the label
dried grape wine aged in sealed caratelli; Occhio di Pernice is the Sangiovese version

the regional catch-all under which the Super Tuscans are sold
tiers: Chianti Classico DOCG

Sangiovese 80 to 100 per cent, no white grapes since 2006; Annata released from 1 October of the year after harvest, Riserva 24 months, Gran Selezione 30 months from estate fruit; the black rooster seal.
Gran Selezione from the 2027 vintage
At least 90 per cent Sangiovese, only native partners, and one of eleven UGA names on the label; voted by the consortium in 2021 and since written into the rules.
Chianti DOCG

Sangiovese at least 70 per cent, white grapes still allowed to 10 per cent; seven sub-zones: Rufina, Colli Senesi, Colli Fiorentini, Colli Aretini, Colline Pisane, Montalbano, Montespertoli; Chianti Superiore is the stricter tier.
Brunello di Montalcino DOCG
100 per cent Sangiovese; at least two years in oak and four months in bottle, released from 1 January of the fifth year after harvest; Riserva six months in bottle and the sixth year.
Rosso di Montalcino DOC
100 per cent Sangiovese from the same zone, released from 1 September of the year after harvest; the earlier glass.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano DOCG
Sangiovese (Prugnolo Gentile) at least 70 per cent; two years of ageing, three for the Riserva; Rosso di Montepulciano DOC beneath it and the Pieve tier above.
Pieve (Vino Nobile)

Published in 2025 and first sold that year from the 2021 vintage: at least 85 per cent Sangiovese with native red partners only, estate grown fruit from one named pieve zone, vines at least fifteen years old, three years of ageing with at least a year in wood and a year in bottle.
Bolgheri DOC
Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Cabernet Franc each allowed to 100 per cent, with Syrah and Sangiovese as partners; Bolgheri Superiore carries two years of ageing with at least one in oak.
Bolgheri Sassicaia DOC
A DOC for one estate since 2013: at least 80 per cent Cabernet Sauvignon, at least two years of ageing, most of it in barrique.
Vernaccia di San Gimignano DOCG
A DOC in 1966, in the first group of Italian DOCs, and a DOCG since 1993; Vernaccia at least 85 per cent; Tuscany's only white DOCG.
Carmignano DOCG
Sangiovese at least 50 per cent with Cabernet Sauvignon or Franc required at 10 to 20 per cent; a zone named in the Medici decree of 1716; DOC 1975, DOCG 1990.
Morellino di Scansano DOCG
Sangiovese at least 85 per cent from the Maremma hills around Scansano; DOCG since 2007.
Toscana IGT
The regional IGT, created under the 1992 law; home of the Super Tuscans, which are top wines sold below DOC by choice.

made.viticulture: Sangiovese is a difficult vine: vigorous, late to ripen, thin skinned enough to rot in an October rain and loose in colour when overcropped. The modern answer, worked out in the Chianti Classico 2000 project from 1987, was better clones, denser planting and lower yields per vine. Training is mostly spurred cordon or Guyot. Altitude is the quality lever inland: Chianti Classico and Rufina keep their best Sangiovese between 350 and 550 metres, where cold nights hold the acid, while Montalcino ripens fully even on its warm southern flank. Sangiovese is picked from late September into October, Merlot earlier on the coast and Cabernet Sauvignon later. Vin Santo grapes are picked healthy and laid on mats to dry for months. Organic farming is widespread in Chianti Classico; drought and hail now matter most.
made.winemaking: Chianti Classico is at least 80 per cent Sangiovese, fermented and aged in anything from large Slavonian botti to French barrique; the traditional houses hold to the big cask and the sour cherry it preserves. Brunello is all Sangiovese and spends at least two years in oak, released only in the fifth year after harvest, so large neutral casks are the norm. Bolgheri works like Bordeaux: fermentation by variety and parcel, malolactic in barrique, blending after a year, 18 to 24 months in French oak for the Superiore and for Sassicaia. The Super Tuscans of the 1970s brought barrique, Cabernet and the end of white grapes in red wine; Chianti Classico banned them from the 2006 vintage. Vin Santo ferments slowly in small sealed caratelli with the madre, the yeast rich lees of the previous batch, and ages three years or more in a warm loft; Occhio di Pernice is the Sangiovese version.

places.name: Chianti Classico
places.note: The historic zone between Florence and Siena, its own DOCG since 1996 under the consortium of 1924: Sangiovese at 250 to 600 metres on galestro and alberese. Greve, Radda, Gaiole and Castellina lie wholly inside it with parts of four more communes; the eleven UGAs add Panzano, Lamole, Montefioralle, Vagliagli and San Donato in Poggio to those names.

places.name: Castelnuovo Berardenga
places.note: The southernmost commune, warmest and lowest towards Siena, where Sangiovese ripens fullest; a UGA in its own name and the home of Fèlsina.

places.name: Panzano in Chianti
places.note: A south facing amphitheatre, the Conca d'Oro, within Greve; a UGA of the 2021 reform and the source of several of the zone's most prized pure Sangiovese wines.

places.name: Radda in Chianti
places.note: High and cool, around 500 metres, for the most perfumed and taut Sangiovese; Le Pergole Torte is the pure Sangiovese IGT of the village.

places.name: Gaiole in Chianti
places.note: The Brolio side of the zone, where the Ricasoli formula for Chianti was written in 1872; Castello di Brolio and Castello di Ama.

places.name: Chianti DOCG and its sub-zones
places.note: The wider ring around the Classico zone, Sangiovese at 70 per cent minimum with white grapes still allowed to 10 per cent; seven named sub-zones, Rufina the one to know and Colli Senesi the largest.

places.name: Chianti Rufina
places.note: The smallest and highest sub-zone, in the Sieve valley northeast of Florence and cooled by Apennine air: long lived Sangiovese, with the Pomino DOC enclave of Chardonnay and Pinot Nero inside it.

places.name: Montalcino
places.note: A hilltop town south of Siena, sheltered by Monte Amiata, warmer and drier than Chianti; Brunello was a DOC in 1966 and a DOCG in 1980, all Sangiovese. The higher north and east slopes on galestro give finesse; the warm south towards Sant'Angelo in Colle gives the fullest wines.

places.name: Sant'Angelo in Colle
places.note: The southwestern village at the warm end of the zone, the source of ripe, generous Brunello from the hills around Il Poggione.

places.name: Montepulciano
places.note: A hill town southeast of Siena above the Val di Chiana, lower and sandier than Montalcino; Vino Nobile, a DOCG from 1980, is Sangiovese called Prugnolo Gentile at 70 per cent minimum, with Rosso di Montepulciano beneath and the Pieve tier, first released in 2025, above. The Abruzzo grape shares the name and nothing else.

places.name: Bolgheri
places.note: A village of the commune of Castagneto Carducci on the coast south of Livorno; Cabernet planted here in 1944 became Sassicaia, first sold from the 1968 vintage, and the DOC of 1983 admitted reds in 1994. Alluvial clay, sand and gravel, sea breezes and full ripeness; Masseto's blue clay hill lies beside Ornellaia.

places.name: Bolgheri Sassicaia
places.note: The single estate DOC within Bolgheri since 2013, Tenuta San Guido's Cabernet from the Sassicaia vineyards; the first Super Tuscan and the only one with a DOC of its own.

places.name: Maremma
places.note: The coastal south around Grosseto: Morellino di Scansano DOCG for Sangiovese, Maremma Toscana DOC for everything else, Montecucco towards Monte Amiata and Vermentino on the shore.

places.name: Scansano
places.note: The hill town inland of Grosseto whose Sangiovese is called Morellino; DOCG since 2007 at 85 per cent minimum.

places.name: San Gimignano
places.note: The tower town west of Chianti whose dry Vernaccia took DOC in 1966, in the first group of Italian DOCs and usually taught as the first, and has been Tuscany's only white DOCG since 1993.

places.name: Carmignano
places.note: A small DOCG west of Florence near Prato, protected by the Medici decree of 1716, where Cabernet has been required in the Sangiovese blend since the DOC of 1975.

producers.name: Marchesi Antinori
producers.why: The Florentine house trading since 1385 whose Tignanello of 1971 and Solaia of 1978 defined the Super Tuscan; Guado al Tasso is its Bolgheri estate.

producers.name: Tenuta San Guido
producers.why: Sassicaia: Cabernet planted at Bolgheri in 1944 and sold from the 1968 vintage, the first Super Tuscan, with Guidalberto as its second wine.

producers.name: Biondi-Santi (Tenuta Greppo)
producers.why: The Montalcino estate where Brunello was first bottled as such in 1888 from a selected Sangiovese; long ageing in Slavonian oak, taut and very long lived.

producers.name: Tenuta Il Poggione
producers.why: A Sant'Angelo in Colle estate making classic, generous Brunello aged in large French oak; the reliable Brunello of a restaurant list.

producers.name: Fattoria di Fèlsina
producers.why: Castelnuovo Berardenga's benchmark for pure Sangiovese Chianti Classico, with the single vineyard Rancia Riserva and the IGT Fontalloro.

producers.name: Tenuta dell'Ornellaia
producers.why: Founded at Bolgheri in 1981; Ornellaia is the Bolgheri Superiore flagship and Masseto, from the blue clay hill beside it, is Italy's great Merlot.

producers.name: Castello Banfi
producers.why: The Montalcino estate founded by American importers in 1978 at Sant'Angelo Scalo that took Brunello to the world; also Moscadello and clonal research on Sangiovese.

producers.name: Barone Ricasoli (Castello di Brolio)
producers.why: Castello di Brolio at Gaiole, where the 1872 Ricasoli formula for Chianti was written; the oldest winery name in Chianti Classico.

producers.name: Montevertine
producers.why: The Radda estate whose Le Pergole Torte, pure Sangiovese since 1977, is sold as IGT by choice.

producers.name: Fontodi
producers.why: Panzano's Conca d'Oro, organic; Flaccianello della Pieve is its pure Sangiovese IGT.

producers.name: Isole e Olena
producers.why: A Barberino Tavarnelle estate; Cepparello, pure Sangiovese IGT since 1980, is its flagship.

producers.name: Avignonesi
producers.why: Montepulciano's best known house and the reference for Vin Santo and Occhio di Pernice.

producers.name: Poliziano
producers.why: A Montepulciano estate for modern, polished Vino Nobile.

producers.name: Marchesi Frescobaldi
producers.why: The Florentine family firm with Nipozzano in Rufina, Pomino and Castelgiocondo in Montalcino.

producers.name: Fattoria Selvapiana
producers.why: Rufina's classic estate; the Bucerchiale Riserva proves the sub-zone's ageing power.

producers.name: Soldera (Case Basse)
producers.why: Case Basse at Montalcino, pure Sangiovese sold as Toscana IGT after the estate left the consortium; a cult wine.

producers.name: Poggio di Sotto
producers.why: Castelnuovo dell'Abate; traditional Brunello of great finesse.

producers.name: Tenuta di Capezzana
producers.why: Carmignano's leading estate, Sangiovese with Cabernet and a famous Vin Santo.

producers.name: Montenidoli
producers.why: The San Gimignano estate that showed Vernaccia can age.

producers.name: Castello di Ama
producers.why: A Gaiole estate; single vineyard Chianti Classico Gran Selezione and the Merlot L'Apparita.

producers.name: Le Macchiole
producers.why: Bolgheri; Paleo, a pure Cabernet Franc, and Messorio, a pure Merlot.

producers.name: Grattamacco
producers.why: Bolgheri's second estate, founded in 1977, Bolgheri Superiore with a share of Sangiovese.

producers.name: Casanova di Neri
producers.why: Modern Brunello; Tenuta Nuova and Cerretalto are its single vineyard wines.

terroir.climate: Mediterranean on the coast, continental in the inland hills. Chianti Classico at 250 to 600 metres has hot days, cold nights and cold winters, and its October harvest can meet rain. Montalcino, sheltered by Monte Amiata, is warmer and drier, with the sea some 40 kilometres off. Bolgheri is warm and maritime, cooled by sea breezes, so Cabernet ripens fully. Summer drought, hail and spring frost are the hazards.
terroir.soils: Galestro, a crumbly grey marl that splits like slate, and alberese, a hard pale limestone, are the two words of Chianti Classico; the best Sangiovese sits on their mix, with macigno sandstone in Rufina. Montalcino has galestro and limestone on its higher northern slopes and heavier clay to the south. Montepulciano has sandy clay from an old sea bed. Bolgheri lies on alluvial clay, sand and gravel, with blue clay under Masseto.
terroir.topography: The Apennines wall the north and east, the Tyrrhenian lies west, and between them the land folds into hills. Chianti Classico is a plateau of ridges between Florence and Siena; Montalcino is one hilltop town ringed by vines from roughly 150 to 600 metres; Montepulciano is lower and gentler above the Val di Chiana. Bolgheri is a narrow coastal strip, the Maremma the plain and low hills south of it.
terroir.water: The Arno runs from the Apennines through Florence to Pisa and frames the north; the Sieve valley holds Rufina. The Ombrone drains the Maremma past Grosseto and the Orcia runs south of Montalcino. The Tyrrhenian warms Bolgheri and the Maremma and sends breezes inland as far as Montalcino.

traps: Montepulciano the town makes Vino Nobile from Sangiovese; Montepulciano the grape lives in Abruzzo and never in Vino Nobile.
Chianti Classico is not a sub-zone of Chianti DOCG; it has been a separate DOCG since 1996, and Rufina is a Chianti sub-zone, not a Classico one.
Brunello is 100 per cent Sangiovese and Chianti Classico only 80 per cent minimum; Vino Nobile sits at 70 per cent.
Sassicaia has its own DOC, Bolgheri Sassicaia, since 2013; the other Super Tuscans remain Toscana IGT by choice.
Vernaccia di San Gimignano is a Tuscan white grape; Vernaccia di Oristano in Sardinia is a different grape and a sherry-like wine; and the 1966 DOC was one of the first, usually taught as the first.
Morellino, Brunello and Prugnolo Gentile are all Sangiovese; none is a separate grape.
Vin Santo and Santorini's Vinsanto are different wines, and Vino Santo Trentino is Nosiola from the north.
Super Tuscan is a trade name, not a legal category; tier does not predict price in Tuscany.

wines.note: Sour cherry, dried herbs, leather and dusty tannin over bright acid; medium bodied and made for food. Bistecca alla fiorentina, pappardelle with ragù, pecorino. Riserva and Gran Selezione add depth and oak.
Fuller, warmer and more tannic than Chianti, with dried cherry, tobacco and balsam after long ageing in large oak; it wants a decade and a roast. Rosso di Montalcino is the earlier glass.
Between Chianti Classico and Brunello in weight: plum and cherry, firm tannin and a savoury finish. Pork, game birds and aged cheeses.
Cabernet and Merlot in a Bordeaux shape with Tuscan sun: cassis, Mediterranean herb and ripe tannin; the Superiore carries longer ageing and the estate flagships. Lamb, beef, anything grilled.
Sangiovese with Cabernet, or Cabernet or Merlot alone, aged in barrique and sold as Toscana IGT; Tignanello, Solaia, Masseto and Le Pergole Torte are the names guests ask for.
Dry, lean and faintly bitter, with almond and citrus; the pairing for the town's saffron risotto and for simple fish.
Sangiovese from the Maremma hills: softer, riper and earlier drinking than the inland wines, a by the glass red for cured meats.
Trebbiano and Malvasia dried on mats, then aged for years in small caratelli; amber, nutty and anything from dry to sweet. Served with cantucci, the almond biscuits of Prato.
Moscato Bianco from Brunello's hill, honeyed and floral, made frizzante, still or late harvest; the light end of a Tuscan dessert list.

exam: Montefalco Sagrantino: 100 per cent Sagrantino, DOCG since 1992, 37 months of ageing with 12 in wood, dry or passito; the most tannic grape in Italy.
Orvieto: Grechetto and Trebbiano (Procanico), DOC 1971, shared with Lazio, Classico and Superiore, sweet versions from abboccato to muffa nobile.
Torgiano Rosso Riserva: Sangiovese led DOCG of 1990, three years of ageing, the Lungarotti zone; Torgiano DOC dates from 1968.
Montefalco Rosso is Sangiovese led with a compulsory Sagrantino share; do not call it a lesser Sagrantino.
Umbria's geography: landlocked, no foreign border, Tiber, Lake Trasimeno, Apennines to the east, Tuscany to the west.
The whites by name: Grechetto (Orvieto, Colli Martani), Trebbiano Spoletino (Spoleto), Chardonnay and Grechetto blends as Umbria IGT.
Castello della Sala and its two famous IGT whites are an Umbrian answer, not a Tuscan one, though the Antinori family of Florence has owned the estate since 1940.

grapes.name: Sagrantino
grapes.styles: Montefalco's own grape, thick skinned and small bunched, with the highest tannin and polyphenol load measured in any Italian variety: dry wines of blackberry, dried plum and black tea that need years, and a sweet passito from dried bunches.

grapes.name: Sangiovese
grapes.styles: The workhorse red of the region: the base of Montefalco Rosso, of Torgiano Rosso Riserva and of most of the IGT reds, lighter and more rustic than in Tuscany.

grapes.name: Grechetto
grapes.styles: The white of Orvieto and Colli Martani: thick skinned, resistant to rot, nutty and faintly bitter with pear and white flowers, and the better half of the Orvieto blend. Grechetto di Todi is a separate variety, Pignoletto by another name.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Toscano
grapes.styles: Procanico in Orvieto, where it stretches the Grechetto with neutral, crisp volume; most of the Orvieto blend by history, less of it by choice today.

grapes.name: Trebbiano Spoletino
grapes.styles: A distinct Trebbiano from Spoleto and Montefalco, late ripening and high in acid, often grown up trees in the old way; it gives citrus, herb and salt, sometimes skin fermented.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Permitted in Montefalco Rosso and widely planted for the IGT reds, where it softens Sagrantino and Sangiovese.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A partner in the Umbria IGT reds and in Torgiano's broader DOC; never in Sagrantino.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Grown around Orvieto for barrel fermented whites sold as Umbria IGT, the most famous of them blended with Grechetto.

law.classification: Umbria holds two DOCGs. Torgiano Rosso Riserva was raised in 1990 from the Torgiano DOC of 1968, a Sangiovese led red with three years of ageing; Montefalco Sagrantino followed in 1992 from its 1979 DOC and must be Sagrantino alone, dry (secco) or passito. Around them sit the DOCs: Montefalco for the Sangiovese led Rosso and the Bianco, Orvieto (1971, shared with Lazio) with its Classico heart and Superiore tier, Torgiano for the wider family of wines, Colli Martani for Grechetto, Spoleto for Trebbiano Spoletino, Lago di Corbara and Rosso Orvietano beside Orvieto, Colli del Trasimeno, Colli Perugini, Colli Altotiberini, Amelia (once Colli Amerini), Assisi and Todi. Umbria IGT covers the region, and the cellars use it for Chardonnay, Grechetto blends and Bordeaux grape reds.
labels: wine from dried grapes; Montefalco Sagrantino Passito is the sweet original of the zone
