tiers: Montefalco Sagrantino DOCG
100 per cent Sagrantino; the dry wine ages 37 months with at least 12 in wood and 4 in bottle; the Passito, from dried grapes, shares the DOCG. DOC 1979, DOCG 1992.
Torgiano Rosso Riserva DOCG
Sangiovese led; at least three years of ageing before release; DOC Torgiano 1968, Riserva raised to DOCG in 1990.
Montefalco DOC
Rosso: Sangiovese led with at least 10 per cent Sagrantino, 18 months of ageing, Riserva 30; Bianco a white of Grechetto and Trebbiano.
Orvieto DOC

Grechetto and Procanico (Trebbiano Toscano) at least 60 per cent together; Classico from the hills around the town; Superiore with higher alcohol and lower yields; secco, abboccato, amabile, dolce and the botrytised muffa nobile.
Colli Martani DOC
The Grechetto DOC of the Martani hills south of Perugia; Todi holds a DOC of its own for the Grechetto di Todi vine.
Spoleto DOC
A DOC of 2011 for Trebbiano Spoletino as a still, sparkling or passito white.
Umbria IGT
The regional catch all, where the barrel fermented Chardonnay and Grechetto whites and the Bordeaux blend reds are sold.

made.viticulture: Montefalco's vineyards sit on the ridge and the slopes below the town, mostly spur pruned cordon and Guyot at moderate density, with the old vine training up maple and elm trees surviving in a few Trebbiano Spoletino plots. Sagrantino is a thick skinned grape that resists rot but ripens late; growers leave it into October for the tannin to soften on the vine, and it is picked by hand, with the passito bunches chosen for their looseness so that they dry without mould. Sangiovese and the whites come in weeks earlier. Orvieto's plateau grows Grechetto and Procanico on tuff that drains fast, and the autumn fog in the Paglia valley is what the muffa nobile producers count on. Torgiano's low hills by the Tiber are warm enough to ripen Sangiovese fully. The hazards are spring frost in the basins, hail in summer and, for Sagrantino, a wet October that spoils the drying. Lake Trasimeno's shore gives a gentler climate for the region's Gamay, which is in fact Grenache under a local name.
made.winemaking: Dry Sagrantino is a wine of the 1970s; before that the grape was dried and made sweet for the church calendar. The dry wine is fermented with long maceration, two to four weeks, to extract and begin to polymerise the tannin, then aged in a mix of large casks and barrique for well over a year and held in bottle, because the rules ask thirty-seven months in all before release with at least twelve in wood and four in bottle. The passito is fermented slowly from bunches dried on racks for weeks, often into the winter, and keeps both sugar and a wall of tannin. Montefalco Rosso is made like a Tuscan Sangiovese, with the Sagrantino share giving colour and grip. Orvieto is cool fermented in steel to keep it light, Grechetto often with a short skin contact for texture; the sweet versions are either arrested to leave sugar (abboccato, amabile, dolce) or made from botrytised bunches picked late. Torgiano Rosso Riserva takes three years of ageing before release. Umbria IGT lets the cellar blend Chardonnay with Grechetto in barrel or make Bordeaux style reds.

places.name: Montefalco
places.note: A hill town between Foligno and Spoleto called the balcony of Umbria, whose ridge and four neighbouring communes (Bevagna, Gualdo Cattaneo, Castel Ritaldi and Giano dell'Umbria) grow Sagrantino on clay, limestone and sandy marine deposits. The DOCG covers the dry wine and the passito; the DOC Rosso and Bianco share the same hills.

places.name: Bevagna
places.note: The commune on the plain below Montefalco, inside the DOCG, with lower sites at the edge of the plain.

places.name: Orvieto
places.note: A cathedral town on a tuff cliff above the Paglia, the DOC named for it stretching east along the Tiber and south into Lazio. Classico covers the hills closest to the town; the lower Paglia valley gives the fog for the muffa nobile wines. Antinori's Castello della Sala estate lies inside the zone and sells its Chardonnay and Grechetto whites as Umbria IGT.

places.name: Lago di Corbara
places.note: A DOC of 1998 on the reservoir of the Tiber beside Orvieto, for reds from Sangiovese, Cabernet, Merlot and Pinot Nero.

places.name: Torgiano
places.note: A village at the meeting of the Chiascio and the Tiber south of Perugia, whose DOC of 1968 was one of Italy's early ones and whose Rosso Riserva became a DOCG in 1990; the zone was built almost alone by the Lungarotti house, whose Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio is the reference wine.

places.name: Colli Martani and Todi
places.note: The hills south of Perugia around Todi and Giano dell'Umbria, the DOC home of Grechetto as a varietal white; Grechetto di Todi is a different vine from Grechetto di Orvieto.

places.name: Spoleto
places.note: The Spoleto DOC of 2011 covers the old Trebbiano Spoletino vineyards south of Montefalco, a late ripening white once trained up trees and now the region's most talked about new wine.

places.name: Colli del Trasimeno
places.note: The DOC on the shores of Lake Trasimeno, west of Perugia, for Sangiovese reds, Grechetto whites and the local Gamay del Trasimeno, which is Grenache.

places.name: Lazio, the neighbour to the south
places.note: The sheet carries no Lazio locator, so its wines sit here: Frascati from the volcanic Castelli Romani hills south of Rome (Malvasia and Trebbiano, Frascati Superiore and Cannellino di Frascati at DOCG since 2011), Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone on Lake Bolsena, Cesanese del Piglio DOCG for the region's native red, and the Lazio side of the Orvieto DOC.

producers.name: Arnaldo Caprai
producers.why: The estate that made dry Sagrantino a modern wine through clonal research with the University of Milan from the late 1980s; its 25 Anni bottling is the zone's best known label.

producers.name: Paolo Bea
producers.why: A small Montefalco family estate working without additions, long macerations and late release: the natural wine reference for Sagrantino and Montefalco Rosso.

producers.name: Lungarotti
producers.why: The house that built Torgiano from the 1960s, won it a DOC in 1968 and its Rosso Riserva a DOCG in 1990; Rubesco Riserva Vigna Monticchio is the wine.

producers.name: Castello della Sala
producers.why: Antinori's Orvieto estate, whose barrel fermented Cervaro della Sala (Chardonnay with Grechetto) and botrytised Muffato della Sala showed what Umbria IGT could be.

producers.name: Adanti
producers.why: One of the early estates of dry Sagrantino, at Arquata near Bevagna, known for classic, slow Montefalco.

producers.name: Antonelli San Marco
producers.why: A Montefalco estate of 1881 known for restrained, organic Sagrantino and a serious Trebbiano Spoletino.

producers.name: Tabarrini
producers.why: Single vineyard Sagrantino from Montefalco's Turrita side and a textured Trebbiano Spoletino; a grower's estate of the new generation.

producers.name: Decugnano dei Barbi
producers.why: An Orvieto Classico estate on the Corbara side that revived botrytised Orvieto and makes a metodo classico sparkling from the same hills.

producers.name: Barberani
producers.why: Organic Orvieto Classico Superiore from the Corbara shore, with the Calcaia muffa nobile as its sweet flagship.

terroir.climate: Continental with a Mediterranean summer: hot, dry days from June to September, cold winters and real spring frost risk in the valleys. The Apennines to the east shut out the Adriatic, so Umbria is more continental and more sharply seasonal than coastal Tuscany; Lake Trasimeno softens its own shore. Montefalco's long autumn lets Sagrantino hang into October to ripen its tannin.
terroir.soils: Clay and limestone on the Montefalco ridge, with sandy marine deposits and pebbles on its slopes. Orvieto sits on a cliff of volcanic tuff, the ash of the Vulsini volcanoes, with clay and sand beneath it. Torgiano works alluvial clay and sand where the Chiascio meets the Tiber. Lake Trasimeno's shore is light clay and sand over limestone.
terroir.topography: A land of hills and small basins: the Tiber valley runs the length of it, the Valle Umbra opens below Assisi, Spoleto and Montefalco, and the Apennine ridge walls the east. Montefalco's vineyards climb the slopes below a hill town of about 470 metres that looks over the whole plain. Orvieto's zone is a tuff plateau cut by the Paglia valley.
terroir.water: The Tiber is the spine, fed by the Chiascio at Torgiano and the Paglia at Orvieto; the Corbara reservoir on the Tiber gives Lago di Corbara DOC its name. Lake Trasimeno, the largest lake of peninsular Italy, moderates the vineyards of the Colli del Trasimeno DOC on its shores.

traps: Sagrantino di Montefalco and Montefalco Sagrantino name the same DOCG; the second is the form the rules use today.
Montefalco Rosso is a Sangiovese blend; Montefalco Sagrantino is pure Sagrantino. The DOC and the DOCG share a town, not a grape rule.
Orvieto is a white wine zone; Rosso Orvietano and Lago di Corbara are the separate red DOCs beside it.
Grechetto di Orvieto and Grechetto di Todi are two different vines; the Todi one is Emilia's Pignoletto.
Gamay del Trasimeno is Grenache, not the Beaujolais grape.
The Orvieto DOC crosses into Lazio; Umbria shares it rather than owning it outright.
Trebbiano Spoletino is a separate variety, not Trebbiano Toscano grown near Spoleto.

wines.note: Opaque, black fruited and fiercely tannic, with dried plum, cocoa and black tea; it is held in wood and bottle for over three years before sale and still wants a decade. Decant and serve with roast lamb, wild boar or aged pecorino.
The original form: bunches dried for weeks, then fermented into a sweet, tannic red of fig and blackberry. The local match is the Easter lamb or a dark chocolate cake, poured in a small glass.
Sangiovese led with a measured share of Sagrantino for grip: cherry, dried herbs and firm tannin, ready years before the Sagrantino is. The everyday red of the zone, with pasta and grilled sausages.

Grechetto and Trebbiano, dry and light to medium in weight, with pear, almond and a bitter twist; Classico from the hills around the town, Superiore with more ripeness. Lake fish, fritto misto and the region's black truffle dishes.

A botrytised Orvieto from the foggy valleys by the Paglia and Lake Corbara, golden and honeyed with apricot and saffron; the abboccato and amabile styles are its lighter, older cousins. Serve with blue cheese or fruit tarts.
Sangiovese led, aged at least three years and built to last: sour cherry, leather and tobacco with a firm, dry finish. Pigeon, game birds and braised beef.
Bright and saline, lemon peel and bitter herbs, sometimes amber from time on the skins; a newer white sold under the Spoleto DOC or as IGT. Grilled fish, strangozzi with truffle, fresh cheeses.

Valpolicella's blend and its four methods: Valpolicella, Ripasso, Amarone (dry), Recioto (sweet).
Amarone: appassimento, minimum alcohol, ageing, DOCG since 2010; Classico's five communes.
Soave: Garganega 70% minimum, Classico's volcanic hills, Soave Superiore and Recioto di Soave DOCG.
Bardolino and Chiaretto on Garda; Lugana shared with Lombardy.

grapes.name: Glera
grapes.styles: The Prosecco grape, itself called Prosecco until 2009: pear, white flowers and green apple, made sparkling in tank to keep that freshness; at least 85% of any Prosecco.

grapes.name: Garganega
grapes.styles: Soave's grape, at least 70% of the blend: lemon, almond and a saline stone, late ripening on pergolas; dried, it makes Recioto di Soave.

grapes.name: Corvina
grapes.styles: The lead of Valpolicella, Amarone and Bardolino: sour cherry, thick skins that dry well, moderate tannin. Corvinone, a separate larger-berried grape, may replace up to half of its share.

grapes.name: Rondinella
grapes.styles: Valpolicella's reliable second grape, 5 to 30%: neutral but disease resistant and good for drying.

grapes.name: Molinara
grapes.styles: Once compulsory in Valpolicella, now optional; pale and high in acid, it lightened the blend.

grapes.name: Oseleta
grapes.styles: A tiny-berried, tannic local red revived for colour and grip in Valpolicella blends.

grapes.name: Trebbiano di Soave
grapes.styles: Soave's permitted partner, genetically Verdicchio; adds acid.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grown in volume on the plain for Delle Venezie DOC, the three-region Pinot Grigio denomination created in 2017.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Pinot Nero gives Prosecco DOC Rosé its 10 to 15% and its red fruit, a category created in 2020.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Up to 15% in Prosecco and the base of some Lessini sparkling.

grapes.name: Durella
grapes.styles: The searingly acid white of the Lessini hills, made into traditional method Lessini Durello.

grapes.name: Raboso
grapes.styles: A dark, tannic, high-acid red of the Piave plain; Piave Malanotte is its DOCG.

grapes.name: Moscato Giallo
grapes.styles: Fior d'Arancio in the Colli Euganei, sweet sparkling and passito.

grapes.name: Tai
grapes.styles: Friulano's Veneto name since 2007; Lison DOCG shares it with Friuli.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: The most planted red on the Venetian plain, for soft everyday wine.

law.classification: Veneto's denominations fall into three families. Prosecco is a pyramid: Prosecco DOC across nine provinces of Veneto and Friuli, then two hill DOCGs, Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore and Asolo Prosecco, with the Rive (43 named hamlets, vintage dated, hand picked) and Superiore di Cartizze (one hill in Valdobbiadene) at the top. Valpolicella is a ladder of methods on one blend: Valpolicella DOC (and Superiore), Valpolicella Ripasso DOC (its own DOC since 2010), Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG and Recioto della Valpolicella DOCG (both 2010), each available as Classico from the five historic communes or as Valpantena. Soave DOC has Classico and Colli Scaligeri zones, Soave Superiore DOCG and Recioto di Soave DOCG, and since 2019 33 named UGA, the unità geografiche aggiuntive. Bardolino Superiore, Piave Malanotte, Colli di Conegliano, Lison, Recioto di Gambellara, Montello Rosso, Bagnoli Friularo and Colli Euganei Fior d'Arancio complete the DOCG list.
labels: In Valpolicella the five western communes (Negrar, Fumane, Marano, Sant'Ambrogio, San Pietro in Cariano); in Soave the hills of Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone
Valpolicella Superiore: 12% minimum and a year's ageing; Soave Superiore is a DOCG; Prosecco Superiore belongs only to the two hill DOCGs
Valpolicella re-fermented on Amarone or Recioto skins
A single hillside hamlet or commune in Conegliano Valdobbiadene, vintage dated and hand picked; 43 of them
The one hill of 107 hectares in Valdobbiadene at the top of the Prosecco pyramid
In Prosecco, 12 to 17 grams of sugar: sweeter than Brut, the traditional style
Bottle-refermented Prosecco left on its lees, cloudy, undisgorged
A valley subzone of Valpolicella east of the Classico zone, named on the label

made.viticulture: Pergola Veronese, the overhead trellis, is the traditional training of Soave and Valpolicella: it suits Garganega's vigour, shades the fruit in a hot summer and keeps bunches healthy for drying; Guyot has spread for quality still wine. Grapes destined for Amarone and Recioto are chosen in the vineyard, picked early into shallow crates, and must be whole, loose-clustered and sound, because they will spend the autumn in the fruttaio, the drying loft. Prosecco in the DOCG hills is hand picked on slopes so steep the growers call the work heroic, and the Rive bottlings must be hand harvested and vintage dated; the plain is machine picked and high yielding, which keeps the price down. Hazards are hail, downy mildew in humid summers, and rot in the drying lofts if the autumn is damp; the lofts are ventilated and the bunches inspected for the better part of three months.
made.winemaking: Appassimento is the Veneto's method: whole bunches lose around a third of their weight over three to four months, concentrating sugar, acid and glycerol and letting a little botrytis in. Pressed no earlier than December, fermented slowly through the winter to dryness, 14% at the least and usually more, Amarone then ages at least two years (four for Riserva); stopped early with sugar remaining, the same must is Recioto. Ripasso puts finished Valpolicella onto the warm pomace of Amarone or Recioto for a second short fermentation, lifting alcohol and body; the law ties the volume of Ripasso to the Amarone whose skins it uses. Prosecco is made by the Martinotti tank method: second fermentation in sealed pressure tanks, a few weeks on the lees, filtered and bottled under pressure, with sweetness set by residual sugar from Brut Nature to Demi-Sec; col fondo, or sui lieviti, is the old bottle-refermented, cloudy, undisgorged style. Soave is pressed and cold fermented in steel; Classico Riservas see large oak or lees.

places.name: Valpolicella
places.note: The valleys north of Verona between the Adige and the Lessini. Corvina 45 to 95% (Corvinone may stand in for up to half of it), Rondinella 5 to 30%, the rest from other local reds. The same blend makes four wines by method: Valpolicella, Ripasso, Amarone and Recioto.

places.name: Valpolicella Classico
places.note: The original five communes to the west: Negrar, Fumane, Marano di Valpolicella, Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella and San Pietro in Cariano; the great Amarone houses cluster here.

places.name: Negrar
places.note: The largest of the Classico communes, home of the most famous traditional Amarone cellar and of a large cooperative.

places.name: Fumane
places.note: The valley of the La Grola hill and of the Allegrini house.

places.name: Sant'Ambrogio di Valpolicella
places.note: The western edge of the Classico zone towards the Adige and Garda, the marble quarry country of Valpolicella.

places.name: Valpantena
places.note: The valley directly north of Verona, east of the Classico zone, with its own label mention; the Bertani house's home.

places.name: Valpolicella orientale
places.note: The eastern valleys of Illasi, Mezzane and Tramigna: cooler and later, with a modern reputation for dense Amarone.

places.name: Soave
places.note: The hills and plain around Soave and Monteforte d'Alpone, east of Verona. Garganega at least 70%, with Trebbiano di Soave and Chardonnay allowed for the rest. Classico is the hill core; Colli Scaligeri the other hills; the plain makes the volume.

places.name: Soave Classico
places.note: Volcanic basalt on the Monteforte side, limestone around Soave's castle; the age-worthy wines, from pergola-trained old vines.

places.name: Monteforte d'Alpone
places.note: The volcanic commune: Foscarino and Froscà among the UGA.

places.name: Prosecco
places.note: Prosecco DOC spans nine provinces across Veneto and Friuli; Treviso and Trieste may appear on the label as subzones. The hills north of Treviso hold the two DOCGs.

places.name: Conegliano Valdobbiadene
places.note: The senior DOCG between the two towns, listed by UNESCO in 2019 for its steep hogback hills, with 43 Rive and the Cartizze hill.

places.name: Cartizze
places.note: A single hill of 107 hectares above Valdobbiadene between San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol; the most expensive Prosecco land, traditionally made Dry.

places.name: Rive
places.note: The 43 named hamlets or communes; each bottle vintage dated and hand harvested.

places.name: Asolo
places.note: The smaller Prosecco DOCG west of the Piave around the hill town of Asolo, with its own Superiore.

places.name: Treviso
places.note: A subzone of Prosecco DOC; the plain's name on a label.

places.name: Bardolino
places.note: Garda's eastern shore on moraine: light Corvina reds, Bardolino Superiore DOCG and the pale Chiaretto di Bardolino rosé.

places.name: Custoza
places.note: South of Garda, a white blend of Garganega, Trebbiano, Tai and Cortese among others, on glacial moraine.

places.name: Lugana
places.note: The Garda south shore shared with Lombardy, where most of the zone lies; Turbiana on white clay.

places.name: Gambellara
places.note: The Garganega hills next door to Soave in the province of Vicenza, with Recioto di Gambellara DOCG.

places.name: Lessini Durello
places.note: Volcanic hills between Verona and Vicenza; Durella makes traditional method sparkling of fierce acidity.

places.name: Colli Euganei
places.note: Volcanic cones south of Padua: Bordeaux reds, Moscato Giallo as Fior d'Arancio DOCG, and Serprino, the local frizzante Glera.

places.name: Breganze
places.note: North of Vicenza: Vespaiolo, whose dried grapes make the sweet Torcolato.

places.name: Piave
places.note: The plain along the Piave east of Treviso: Raboso's Piave Malanotte DOCG and much Merlot.

places.name: Lison
places.note: Tai, which is Friulano, as a DOCG on the plain straddling Veneto and Friuli.

producers.name: Giuseppe Quintarelli
producers.why: Negrar's legend of Amarone and Recioto: long drying, long cask ageing, hand-written labels; the benchmark of traditional Valpolicella.

producers.name: Allegrini
producers.why: Fumane house that led the modern, Guyot-trained, single-vineyard Valpolicella: La Grola and the all-Corvina La Poja.

producers.name: Masi
producers.why: Gargagnago house whose Campofiorin (1964) brought the Ripasso technique to market and whose Costasera carried Amarone abroad.

producers.name: Bertani
producers.why: Founded 1857 in the Valpantena, among the first to sell Amarone from the late 1950s, with a famous library of old vintages.

producers.name: Tedeschi
producers.why: Pedemonte house known for the single-vineyard Monte Olmi Amarone.

producers.name: Bolla
producers.why: The Verona house, founded 1883, that put Soave and Valpolicella on American tables.

producers.name: Pieropan
producers.why: The Soave Classico house that proved Garganega ages: Calvarino and La Rocca since the 1970s.

producers.name: Inama
producers.why: Soave Classico from the volcanic Foscarino hill, plus Carmenère on the Colli Berici.

producers.name: Anselmi
producers.why: The Monteforte house that left the Soave DOC in 2000 to sell its Garganega as IGT in protest at the zone's rules.

producers.name: Gini
producers.why: Monteforte grower on old pergola vines; Contrada Salvarenza.

producers.name: Suavia
producers.why: Soave Classico from the high volcanic sites of Fittà.

producers.name: Bisol
producers.why: Valdobbiadene grower house with a long holding on Cartizze; Cartizze and the Rive bottlings.

producers.name: Nino Franco
producers.why: Valdobbiadene house founded 1919 that led the dry, vintage Prosecco movement: Rustico and the single-site Grave di Stecca.

producers.name: Carpenè Malvolti
producers.why: Conegliano house founded 1868 that first made Prosecco sparkling; its founder set up Italy's first school of oenology in Conegliano in 1876.

terroir.climate: Warm continental on the plain, moderated by Lake Garda to the west and the Adriatic to the south-east, with the Alps and the pre-Alpine Lessini and Treviso hills blocking the north. Valpolicella's valleys draw cool air down from the Lessini at night; the Prosecco hills are wetter and cooler than the plain; summers are hot and humid enough that mildew and hail are the daily worries.
terroir.soils: Soave Classico is volcanic basalt on the Monteforte side and limestone on the Soave side, two faces that give smoke and stone respectively. Valpolicella's hills are limestone and marl with volcanic patches towards the Valpantena and the east; the plain is alluvial gravel and clay. The Conegliano Valdobbiadene hills are marl, sandstone and moraine on steep, eroded slopes. The Colli Euganei are extinct volcanoes; Custoza and Bardolino sit on glacial moraine left by the Garda glacier.
terroir.topography: A band of pre-Alpine hills along the north, the flat Po and Adige plain to the south and Garda on the western edge. Valpolicella is a fan of parallel valleys (the five Classico communes, then Valpantena, then the eastern valleys) running south out of the Lessini into Verona. Soave and Gambellara sit in the hills east of the city; Conegliano Valdobbiadene and Asolo climb steep hogback ridges north of Treviso, with Cartizze a single sheltered hillside.
terroir.water: Lake Garda, the largest in Italy, moderates Bardolino, Custoza and the western Valpolicella; the Adige flows past Verona; the Piave crosses the Prosecco country; the Venetian lagoon closes the east. Water gives the west its mildness and the east its humidity.

traps: Amarone is dry, Recioto is sweet; both come from the same dried grapes. The old chapter line is right.
Prosecco is a place and a method, Glera the grape since 2009; the village of Prosecco is in Friuli near Trieste, not in Veneto.
Extra Dry Prosecco is sweeter than Brut; Dry is sweeter still. Read the scale the other way from Champagne habits.
Ripasso is not made from dried grapes; it is normal Valpolicella passed over Amarone's spent skins.
Soave is a town and Garganega the grape; Soave Classico is a zone, Soave Superiore a separate DOCG, and the two do not mean the same thing.
Corvinone is its own variety, not a clone of Corvina; Molinara is no longer compulsory.
Valpolicella Superiore is a still wine with a year's age, not a Ripasso; Amarone Riserva takes four years.
Lugana belongs mostly to Lombardy; Bardolino and Custoza are the Veneto side of Garda.

wines.note: Glera, tank method, dry to off-dry, pear and white flowers, light and fresh at around 11%; the DOC is the ocean, the DOCGs the hills. Most is Brut or Extra Dry; serve cold, often in a spritz.
The hill DOCG: finer, more floral, sometimes vintage dated from a single Rive, with Superiore di Cartizze at the peak.
Glera with Pinot Nero, vintage dated, 60 days minimum in tank, Brut Nature to Extra Dry; a category since 2020.
Garganega: dry, light to medium, lemon, pear, almond and a chalky or smoky finish; Classico from the hills ages a decade. Risotto, lake fish, white asparagus.
The fresh red: sour cherry, almond, light tannin, drunk young and cool; Superiore is a year older and a shade more serious.
Valpolicella re-fermented on the skins of Amarone: fuller, rounder, dried-fruit tones, the stepping stone between the two.

Dried grapes fermented dry to 14% at the least and usually 15 or more: black cherry, fig, chocolate, bitter almond, velvet tannin, high alcohol. Serve just below room temperature with braised beef, game or hard aged cheese, never with delicate food.
The sweet ancestor of Amarone: the same dried grapes with fermentation halted, red, lush, for chocolate and blue cheese.
Garganega dried on racks into a golden, honeyed sweet wine; Veneto's first DOCG, in 1998.
Corvina-led, pale and light from Garda's eastern shore, served cool; Chiaretto di Bardolino is its pale rosé.
A blended white from the moraine south of Garda, easy and floral, for an aperitivo.
Durella bottle fermented in the volcanic Lessini hills: sharp, mineral, long on the lees.
